title: Senior's toolkit: migrations from laptop to production
summary: The dotnet ef migrations commands, idempotent scripts and bundles for CI, rolling back, and catching a forgotten migration.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: migrations from laptop to production
steps.body: Migrations are easy on a laptop and dangerous in production. Teams generate them locally, review the SQL, and let the pipeline apply them, never the app on start-up. These are the commands that make that work.

toolkit.what: Compare the model with the last snapshot and write a migration class for the difference. Always read it: a rename can come out as drop plus add.
flags: the project that holds the DbContext and migrations
the project whose configuration and services are used
toolkit.example: dotnet ef migrations add AddOrderNotes --project src/Shop.Data --startup-project src/Shop.Api -o Migrations

toolkit.what: Every migration, and which ones are still pending on the database the tools connect to.
flags: check a different database than the configured one
list from the code only, without a database

toolkit.what: Delete the last migration and put the snapshot back. Only for a migration nobody else has applied yet.
flags: also revert it on your local database if you already applied it

toolkit.what: Write the SQL for the migrations. An idempotent script checks the history table first, so it is safe to run on a database at any version. This is what you review and what CI applies.
flags: each migration runs only if it has not been applied
only the migrations between two names, for example `AddRating AddOrderNotes`

toolkit.what: Build one executable that applies the migrations. CI builds it once and the deploy step runs it against each environment.
flags: runs on a machine without the .NET SDK
(when running the bundle) the target database
toolkit.example:
dotnet ef migrations bundle --self-contained -r linux-x64 -o efbundle
./efbundle --connection "$DB_CONNECTION"

toolkit.what: Apply migrations to the database. With a migration name it moves to exactly that version, rolling back newer ones; `0` removes them all.
flags: go to this migration, up or down
target a database other than the configured one
toolkit.when: your own dev database; production gets the reviewed script or bundle

toolkit.what: Fail if the model has changes that no migration captures yet. Put it in CI so a forgotten `migrations add` breaks the build, not the deploy. In code: `db.Database.HasPendingModelChanges()`.
flags: non-zero when a migration is missing

steps.prompt: You added a `Notes` column to `Order`. Put the steps from your laptop to production in order.
lines: Read the generated migration and fix anything that drops data
dotnet ef database update (on your dev database) and run the tests
Commit the migration, the snapshot and the code together
CI: dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent -o migrate.sql
Deploy: apply migrate.sql, then roll out the new app version

steps.prompt: You renamed `Customer.Name` to `Customer.FullName`. The generated migration looks like this. What do you do before merging?
options: Replace both lines with `migrationBuilder.RenameColumn(name: "Name", table: "Customers", newName: "FullName");`, or every customer's name is lost
Nothing: EF Core copies the data across automatically
Run `dotnet ef migrations remove` and give up on the rename
Apply it and restore the names from a backup afterwards
steps.explain: EF Core cannot tell a rename from a delete plus an add, so it sometimes generates the destructive version. Reading every migration before merging is the habit that catches it.

steps.prompt: Match each option to what it does.
pairs: the script is safe on a database at any version
the project whose configuration and services are used
the folder for the migration files
runs where the .NET SDK is not installed

steps.prompt: The CI step that produces the reviewed SQL for deployment.

The API runs on four instances and calls `db.Database.Migrate()` at start-up. After a deploy with a slow migration (an index on a big table), the instances fail their health checks, get restarted, and the rollout loops. What is the usual fix?
options: Apply migrations once from the pipeline (idempotent script or bundle) before the new version rolls out, and remove `Migrate()` from start-up
The connection string is wrong on two instances
SQL Server cannot run migrations in parallel, so use SQLite
steps.explain: Start-up migration ties the schema change to the app's start, needs the app to hold DDL rights, and a failure takes the app down. (EF Core 9+ takes a lock so instances wait for each other instead of colliding, which makes the start-up delay worse, not better.) One controlled step in the deploy is safer and can be reviewed. Never mix `EnsureCreated` with migrations.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Read every generated migration before you commit it, and add `has-pending-model-changes` to CI so a missing one fails the build. In production, apply a reviewed idempotent script or a bundle from the pipeline, never `Migrate()` on start-up.
